CausalChain: Intermittent Fasting -> Energy Stress in HCC Cells -> Activation/Restoration of miR-199a-5p and Induction of miR-202 (and related miRNAs) -> Direct Downregulation of Glycolytic Enzymes HK2 and PKM2 -> Rebalancing: Partial Suppression of Aerobic Glycolysis and Supported Oxidative Phosphorylation -> Reduced Lactate Production -> Attenuated Lactate-Mediated Immune Suppression -> Enhanced Anti-Tumor Immunity and Increased Sorafenib Sensitivity
Hypothesis: We propose that in HCC, intermittent fasting establishes an energy-stressed tumor microenvironment that triggers an adaptive miRNA response, notably restoring miR-199a-5p levels and inducing miR-202 along with other miRNAs. This network directly targets key glycolytic enzymes HK2 and PKM2, thereby rebalancing the metabolic phenotype of HCC cells—not by completely switching from aerobic glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation, but by partially suppressing the Warburg effect while permitting controlled OXPHOS activity. This moderated metabolic reprogramming results in lowered lactate production, which alleviates lactate-driven immune evasion, reactivates anti-tumor immune mechanisms, and enhances the efficacy of sorafenib treatment. This hypothesis will be tested through CRISPR-based gene editing, high-resolution single-cell metabolomic analyses, cutting-edge imaging techniques, and detailed immunophenotyping to establish the causal links and translational relevance of this metabolic-immune axis in HCC.
Abstract: In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), we hypothesize that intermittent fasting initiates a calibrated energy stress response that activates an adaptive miRNA network—centered on the restoration of miR-199a-5p and the induction of additional metabolic regulators such as miR-202—to fine-tune glycolytic enzyme expression. Rather than driving a complete metabolic shift solely toward oxidative phosphorylation, this miRNA-mediated modulation rebalances cancer cell metabolism by partially dampening aerobic glycolysis (via direct suppression of HK2 and PKM2) while supporting controlled oxidative phosphorylation. This dual adjustment minimizes excessive lactate accumulation, thereby reducing lactate-driven immunosuppression and potentiating anti-tumor immune responses, which in turn increases sorafenib sensitivity. To rigorously assess these interconnected pathways, we propose leveraging state-of-the-art technologies including CRISPR-based screens for target validation, high-resolution single-cell metabolomics to monitor dynamic metabolic flux, advanced imaging modalities, and comprehensive immunophenotyping. Such integrative approaches will elucidate the precise, time-resolved causal links from fasting-induced energy stress to metabolic reprogramming and immune modulation in HCC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that intermittent fasting in HCC restores miR-199a-5p and induces miR-202 leading to a direct shift from the Warburg effect to enhanced oxidative phosphorylation, thereby lowering lactate and improving anti-tumor immunity and sorafenib sensitivity. In our revised hypothesis, we address critical review observations by introducing a more nuanced metabolic reprogramming: instead of a full metabolic switch, fasting induces a balanced reprogramming that partially suppresses glycolysis while supporting necessary oxidative phosphorylation. This recalibration minimizes lactate without causing an overall suppression of mitochondrial activity (as noted in competing studies) and integrates advanced methodologies (e.g., single-cell metabolomics, CRISPR screens) to resolve the dynamic and context-dependent regulation of these pathways at a high resolution. Each step of the original causal chain is maintained but is refined to reflect a more adaptive and quantifiable metabolic modulation, ensuring logical coherence and improved experimental practicability.
